subject: History
context: Choose the correct option from the given options and complete the sentences.
stem: The earliest museum in the world was discovered in the excavations at the city of ____.
solution: Ur. The world's earliest known museum was found during the excavations of Ur, an ancient city of Mesopotamia (present-day Iraq). The collection of old and carefully labelled objects gathered there by the Babylonian princess Ennigaldi-Nanna is regarded as the first museum. Delhi, Harappa and Kolkata are not associated with the earliest museum.

subject: History
context: Choose the correct option from the given options and complete the sentences.
stem: In Maharashtra, ____ is supposed to be the first Keertankar.
solution: Saint Namdev. Sant Namdev is regarded as the first Keertankar (performer of Keertan) of Maharashtra; he spread the Bhakti tradition through Keertan, a devotional performing art that combines narration, singing and music. Sant Dnyaneshwar, Sant Eknath and Sant Tukaram came later in the same Varkari tradition.

subject: History
context: Choose the correct option from the given options and complete the sentences.
stem: It may be said that ____ was the founder of modern historiography.
solution: Leopold Ranke. The German historian Leopold von Ranke insisted that history must be written only on the basis of original, authentic documents critically examined by the historian, and that the historian must present the past 'as it actually happened'. This source-based, critical method is the foundation of modern historiography, so Ranke is called its founder. Voltaire pioneered the writing of social and cultural history, Descartes stressed critical scrutiny of documents, and Karl Marx gave the materialist interpretation of history.

subject: History
context: Write short notes (any two).
stem: Write a short note on: Nationalistic Historiography.
solution: Nationalistic historiography is the writing of history from the point of view of one's own nation, with the aim of awakening national pride and self-respect. It arose in India as a reply to the colonial and imperialist historians, who portrayed Indian history as a record of backwardness and justified British rule. Nationalist historians used original sources to show the greatness of India's ancient and medieval past, the achievements of Indian rulers and the exploitative nature of colonial rule. Vishnushastri Chiplunkar, Justice Mahadev Govind Ranade, Vasudev Shastri Khare, Rajwade and Jadunath Sarkar are important names in this tradition; Ranade's writing on the rise of the Maratha power and the studies of the 1857 struggle as India's first war of independence are typical examples. This historiography inspired the freedom movement, though its excessive glorification of the past is also seen as its limitation.

subject: History
context: Write short notes (any two).
stem: Write a short note on: Applied History.
solution: Applied History is the branch of history in which the knowledge of the past is deliberately used for present-day, practical purposes. It does not stop at studying and writing about the past; it makes that knowledge useful to the general public and to society. Applied History is used to conserve and manage historical monuments, forts, caves and other heritage sites, to run museums, archives and libraries, and to plan heritage walks and tourism. It also helps other fields — town planning, archaeology, art, literature, films and serials, advertising, and even administration and law — by supplying reliable information about the past. Because of Applied History, many professional opportunities are available today, such as archaeologist, museologist, archivist, conservator, tour guide and heritage manager. In short, Applied History links the past with the present and makes history a living and useful subject.

subject: History
context: Write short notes (any two).
stem: Write a short note on: Marco Polo.
solution: Marco Polo was a famous traveller and merchant of the thirteenth century who belonged to Venice in Italy. Along with his father and uncle he travelled overland through Persia and Central Asia to China, and stayed for many years at the court of the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan, who employed him on missions in his empire. On his return journey he also travelled by sea and visited the coastal regions of South-East Asia and India. The record of his travels, known as 'The Travels of Marco Polo', gives detailed descriptions of the cities, trade, customs, products and rulers of the lands he saw. His account made the wealth and civilisation of the East known to Europe, encouraged later European explorers, and remains an important source for the history and geography of the period.

subject: History
subtopic: Art, Applied Art and Professional Opportunities
context: Explain the following statements with reasons (any two) :
stem: An expert with deep understanding of art history is required in the art market.
solution: The art market is the field in which paintings, sculptures, antiques and other art objects are bought, sold and auctioned, and where they are valued, insured and exhibited. Before any such object changes hands, someone must decide whether it is genuine or a forgery, to which period, region and school of art it belongs, who created it, and what it is really worth. Only a person with a deep understanding of art history can do this, because such an expert knows the evolution of styles, the materials, colours and techniques used in different periods, and the characteristic features of each artistic tradition, and can therefore date a work and attribute it correctly. Such an expert is also aware of the laws relating to antiquities and of the ethics of the trade, and can prevent the sale of stolen or smuggled objects and the cheating of buyers. Hence an expert with a deep understanding of art history is required in the art market.

subject: History
subtopic: Sources of History, their Conservation and Preservation
context: Explain the following statements with reasons (any two) :
stem: Only trained persons who are duly qualified can take up the tasks involved in the work of conservation and preservation.
solution: Objects of heritage value - manuscripts on paper and palm-leaf, textiles, paintings, coins, metal and stone sculptures, monuments and excavated remains - are old, fragile and chemically sensitive, and any damage caused to them is irreversible because the original object can never be created again. Each material needs its own scientific treatment: the chemicals, cleaning agents, adhesives, temperature and humidity that suit stone will ruin paper or textile. The work therefore demands a knowledge of chemistry, of the technology of the material, of climate control and of methods of documentation, along with the professional ethic of minimum intervention, that is, of never adding anything that alters the original. It also demands a knowledge of the laws relating to antiquities and monuments. A person without such training is likely to destroy the very object he means to save. Therefore only trained persons who are duly qualified can take up the tasks involved in the work of conservation and preservation.

subject: History
context: Explain the following statements with reasons (any two) :
stem: Historical research was driven to focus in depth on various aspects of women's life.
solution: Older historical writing was largely political and dynastic and was written mainly by men, so it dealt with kings, wars and states, and women remained almost invisible in it. In the twentieth century the women's movement and the rise of feminist thought questioned this one-sided picture. Simone de Beauvoir's book 'The Second Sex' (1949) argued that womanhood is not natural but is constructed by society, and this idea forced scholars to re-examine the past from the point of view of women. As a result historians began to study in depth the family, marriage, motherhood, the household, women's labour and property rights, women's participation in movements and their place in religion, education and art. In India too, writings such as those of Sharmila Rege on the narratives of Dalit women brought out the experience of women who had been left out even by earlier accounts. Because of this new perspective, historical research was driven to focus in depth on various aspects of women's life.

subject: History
context: Explain the following statements with reasons (any two) :
stem: Expertise in history is important in the film industry.
solution: A large number of films, serials and documentaries are based on historical themes and on the lives of historical personalities. To make such a film convincing, everything shown on the screen must belong to the period of the story - the costumes, ornaments, hair-styles, weapons, coins, vehicles, utensils, furniture, architecture of the forts and palaces, the language spoken, the customs, rituals and social manners of the time. Only a person who has studied history can supply this information, check the script for factual mistakes and guide the art director, the costume designer and the set designer. A historian is also needed to search archives, old photographs, paintings and documents for making documentaries, and to advise so that a film does not distort facts and hurt public sentiment. Historians therefore work in the film industry as researchers, script consultants and advisers on art direction and costume, and expertise in history is important in the film industry.

subject: History
subtopic: Sources of History, their Conservation and Preservation
context:
Read the following passage and answer the questions based on it :

Sohagaura Copper-Plate : The copper-plate was found at Sohagaura (District Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh). It is supposed to be from the Mauryan period. The inscription on it is in Brahmi Script. The symbols known as 'Tree-in-railing' and 'Mountain' at the beginning of the inscription also occur on punch marked coins. Another symbol which looks like a structure erected on four pillars is supposed to be indicative of a granary. The inscription records a royal order that the grains stored in the granary should be distributed carefully. It is supposed to be suggestive of precautions taken in the times of a famine.
stem: Write the historical importance of Sohagaura copper-plate.
solution:
The Sohagaura copper-plate is an inscribed material source, and its historical importance may be stated as follows :
(1) It is a written record of the Mauryan period and its inscription is in the Brahmi script, so it helps us to know the script and the language in use at that time.
(2) The symbols at the beginning of the inscription, known as 'Tree-in-railing' and 'Mountain', also occur on punch-marked coins; this link between the inscription and the coins helps scholars to date the plate and to connect the evidence of epigraphy with that of numismatics.
(3) One symbol on the plate looks like a structure erected on four pillars and is taken to represent a granary, which shows that grain was stored by the state in special store-houses.
(4) The inscription records a royal order that the grain stored in the granary should be distributed carefully. This shows that the administration itself controlled the storage and distribution of food grain, and that precautions were taken in advance against famine.
Thus the copper-plate throws light on the script, the administration, the economy and the famine-relief measures of the Mauryan period.

subject: History
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two) :
stem: Explain the characteristics of the Islamic Architecture in India with examples.
solution:
Islamic architecture came to India with the Turkish and Mughal rulers and gradually blended with Indian traditions to produce the Indo-Islamic style. Its main characteristics are :
(1) Arcuate construction - the true arch and the dome were used in place of the Indian trabeate system of pillar and beam, and lime mortar was used to bind the masonry.
(2) Domes, minarets, tall gateways and chhatris became the chief features of the buildings.
(3) As the depiction of human and animal figures was avoided, decoration was done with geometrical patterns, floral and creeper designs (arabesque) and beautiful calligraphy of verses.
(4) Perforated stone screens (jaali), inlay work of coloured stones (pietra dura), stucco work and glazed tiles were used for ornamentation.
(5) Red sandstone and white marble were the favourite building materials.
(6) Symmetry and balance in the plan, and the laying out of a building in the middle of a char-bagh, that is, a garden divided into four parts by water channels, with fountains and pools.
(7) The typical buildings are mosques with a large open courtyard, the mihrab and the mimbar, tombs, forts and palaces.
Examples : the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, the Qutub Minar and the Alai Darwaza at Delhi, Humayun's tomb, the Jama Masjid and the Red Fort at Delhi, the Taj Mahal and Fatehpur Sikri at Agra, the Gol Gumbaz at Vijapur (Bijapur) and the Charminar at Hyderabad.

subject: History
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two) :
stem: Write about the history of Aakashvani.
solution:
Radio broadcasting in India began with private radio clubs. The Radio Club of Bombay started broadcasting in 1923 and the Calcutta Radio Club was founded soon after. In 1927 the Indian Broadcasting Company began regular broadcasts from its Bombay and Calcutta stations. The company ran into losses, and in 1930 the Government took the service over and named it the Indian State Broadcasting Service. In 1936 it was renamed 'All India Radio', and in 1957 it was given the name 'Aakashvani', a name taken from a poem of the poet Pandit Narendra Sharma.
After independence the network expanded rapidly and stations were opened all over the country. In 1957 the Vividh Bharati service was started for light entertainment and film music, and commercial advertising on it began in 1967. In 1997 Aakashvani was brought under Prasar Bharati, an autonomous corporation, along with Doordarshan.
Aakashvani broadcasts news bulletins, discussions and talks, classical, folk and film music, radio plays, and special programmes for farmers, workers, women, children, students and the armed forces, besides weather reports and warnings during natural calamities. Its rural and agricultural programmes carried scientific farming to the villages, and its educational broadcasts helped schools and universities. Today its broadcasts, including the FM channels, reach almost the entire population of the country in a large number of languages and dialects, and it has thus played an important role in spreading information, education and entertainment and in building national unity.

subject: History
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two) :
stem: Explain the difference between indoor and outdoor games.
solution:
Games are classified as indoor games and outdoor games according to the place where they are played. The differences between them are as follows :

| Indoor games | Outdoor games |
|---|---|
| They are played inside a closed hall, room or covered stadium. | They are played on open grounds, fields, tracks or in open water. |
| They need comparatively little space. | They need a large open space or a big ground. |
| They can be played at any time, as they do not depend on sunlight or on the weather; artificial light can be used. | They depend on daylight and on the weather, and rain or a storm can stop the play. |
| The number of players and of spectators is usually small. | A large number of players and a very large number of spectators can take part or watch. |
| Many of them depend more on concentration, quickness of the hand and mental skill than on running. | They usually demand greater physical stamina, speed, running and team work. |
| Examples : chess, carrom, table tennis, badminton, boxing, wrestling, weight-lifting, gymnastics, billiards. | Examples : cricket, football, hockey, kabaddi, kho-kho, volleyball, tennis, athletics, swimming. |

It should be noted that the line between the two is not rigid. Games such as badminton, basketball, volleyball and swimming are played both indoors and outdoors, and with the building of covered and air-conditioned stadiums many games that were once purely outdoor are now played indoors as well.

subject: History
subtopic: Conservation and Preservation of Historical Places
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two) :
stem: What measures have to be taken for the conservation of the Heritage sites ?
solution:
Heritage sites - forts, caves, temples, monuments and excavated remains - are the property of the whole nation and once destroyed they can never be built again. The following measures have to be taken for their conservation :
(1) Legal protection : the site should be declared a protected monument under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, and the Archaeological Survey of India, the State Department of Archaeology and bodies such as INTACH should look after it. Important sites should be got included in the UNESCO World Heritage List.
(2) Documentation : every site should be surveyed, measured, photographed and mapped, and a detailed record of its present condition should be kept, so that any later damage can be noticed.
(3) Scientific repair : structural repairs and chemical cleaning should be done only by trained conservators, using materials that match the original, and with the least possible interference in the original structure.
(4) Control of the surroundings : encroachment, unauthorised construction and quarrying near the monument must be stopped, and industrial and vehicular pollution has to be controlled, as has been done by creating the Taj Trapezium Zone around the Taj Mahal.
(5) Regulation of visitors : the number of visitors should be regulated, proper pathways, railings, lighting, drinking water and toilets provided, and writing names, scratching, littering and vandalism strictly prohibited.
(6) Prevention of theft and illegal excavation : sculptures and antiquities should be guarded by watchmen and CCTV cameras, and the smuggling of antiquities must be checked.
(7) Protection against disasters : arrangements should be made against fire, flood, earthquake, water seepage and the growth of vegetation on the walls.
(8) Public awareness : students and local people should be taken on heritage walks and educated about the value of the site; if the local community gets employment and income from responsible tourism, it will itself protect the monument.
(9) Adequate funds, trained staff and modern technology such as three-dimensional scanning and drone surveys should be provided for this work.

subject: Political Science
stem: The power to make changes in the Constitution without altering the basic structure of the Constitution lies with ____.
solution: Parliament. Article 368 of the Constitution vests the power of amendment in Parliament. However, in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) the Supreme Court held that while Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution, it cannot alter or destroy its 'basic structure' (supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review). So the amending power without altering the basic structure lies with Parliament — not with the citizens, the President or the Vice-President.

subject: Political Science
subtopic: Farmers' Movement and the Green Revolution
stem: To increase agricultural production and become self-sufficient with regard to food grains, ____ was initiated.
solution: Green revolution. From the mid-1960s India adopted the Green Revolution — high-yielding variety seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides, assured irrigation and mechanised farming — precisely to raise the output of food grains (mainly wheat and rice) and end dependence on imported grain. The White Revolution relates to milk production (Operation Flood), the Industrial Revolution to manufacturing, and 'Water revolution' is not a recognised programme in this context.

subject: Political Science
context: State whether the following statements are true or false. Give reasons for your answers (any two):
setLabel: Q7 True or false with reasons
stem: Policy of reservation of seats is important for the establishment of social justice and equality.
solution: True. Indian society was for centuries divided by caste, and the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other backward sections were kept away from education, property and political power. Formal equality alone cannot undo this historical injustice, because unequals cannot compete equally. The Constitution therefore provides for reservation of seats in legislatures, in government jobs and in educational institutions for these deprived sections (and one-third of the seats for women in local self-government bodies). This gives them actual representation in decision-making and a share in resources, and thus converts equality on paper into equality in practice. Reservation is therefore an instrument of social justice and real equality.

subject: Political Science
context: State whether the following statements are true or false. Give reasons for your answers (any two):
setLabel: Q7 True or false with reasons
stem: The state government decides as to when and in how many stages the elections would be held in a particular state.
solution: False. The conduct of elections to Parliament and to the State Legislatures is entrusted by the Constitution to the Election Commission of India, an independent constitutional body. It is the Election Commission — not the state government — that announces the election programme, fixes the dates of polling and decides in how many phases or stages the polling will be held in a particular state, keeping in mind the size of the electorate and the law-and-order situation. If the ruling government of a state could fix the schedule, it would misuse that power to its own advantage and elections would not remain free and fair. From the announcement of the programme the Model Code of Conduct comes into force and the government machinery works under the Commission's directions.

subject: Political Science
context: State whether the following statements are true or false. Give reasons for your answers (any two):
setLabel: Q7 True or false with reasons
stem: People may lose confidence in the democratic process due to the corruption during elections.
solution: True. Elections are the very foundation of democracy, and their credibility rests on the belief that every vote counts equally. When money power is used to buy votes, when liquor or gifts are distributed, when muscle power is used for booth capturing and bogus voting, and when candidates with a criminal record are given tickets, the result no longer reflects the free will of the voters. The ordinary voter then feels that his single honest vote is meaningless and that whoever spends the most or frightens the most will win. This breeds indifference, falling voter turnout and cynicism about leaders and institutions. Thus corruption during elections directly weakens people's faith in the democratic process.

subject: Political Science
context: Explain the following concepts (any one):
stem: Regionalism
solution: Regionalism means excessive attachment to one's own region, language or culture, placing the interest of that region above the interest of the nation as a whole. It grows out of regional imbalance in development, a distinct linguistic and cultural identity, a feeling of neglect or exploitation by the centre, and 'sons of the soil' sentiment which claims local jobs and resources only for local people. Its expressions include demands for separate statehood, inter-state disputes over river waters and boundaries, and hostility towards migrants from other states. Love of one's own region is natural and can encourage local development, but when regionalism becomes narrow and aggressive it obstructs national integration and threatens the unity and integrity of the country.

subject: Political Science
context: Explain the following concepts (any one):
stem: Women representation in the Lok Sabha.
solution: Women form nearly half of India's population and have equal voting rights, yet their representation in the Lok Sabha has always remained low — from about 5% in the first Lok Sabha to only around 14% in recent Lok Sabhas. The main reasons are the patriarchal structure of society, family responsibilities, lack of money and organisational support, and the reluctance of political parties to give tickets to women. Because law-making bodies frame policies on education, health, safety and employment that directly affect women, their adequate presence in the Lok Sabha is essential for genuine democracy. As a first step the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments reserved one-third of the seats for women in Panchayats and Municipalities, and the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 provides for reservation of one-third of the seats for women in the Lok Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies.

subject: Political Science
subtopic: Characteristics and Functions of Political Parties
context: Do as directed (any one):
stem: Complete the following concept map: the central box reads 'Important characteristics of political parties', and four blank boxes are linked to it. Write one important characteristic of political parties in each of the four boxes.
solution:
Important characteristics of political parties:

1. A definite ideology and programme — every party has its own set of principles, policies and a manifesto placed before the people.
2. An organised structure — a party has enrolled members, office-bearers and leaders working from the local unit up to the national level.
3. Aim of capturing political power — a party contests elections and tries to form the government, or to act as the opposition, through constitutional and peaceful means.
4. Work for public welfare and the national interest — a party claims to promote the welfare of the people, shapes public opinion and links the people with the government.

| Kolam | Adilabad region (present-day Telangana), extending into Yavatmal district of Vidarbha |
| Munda | Chhotanagpur plateau around Ranchi, present-day Jharkhand (led by Birsa Munda) |

These uprisings were the response of tribal communities to the loss of their traditional rights over land and forests, to the exploitation by moneylenders, landlords and contractors, and to the new forest laws of the British.

subject: Political Science
context: Answer the following questions in brief (any one):
stem: Explain the challenges in conducting free and fair elections.
solution:
The Election Commission faces several serious challenges in conducting free and fair elections in India:

1. Money power — enormous and often unaccounted expenditure by candidates and parties, and the distribution of cash, liquor and gifts to buy votes, which makes the contest unequal for an honest candidate.
2. Muscle power and criminalisation — the use of violence, intimidation of voters, booth capturing and bogus voting, and the entry of persons with a criminal record into politics.
3. Misuse of official machinery — the ruling party using government vehicles, offices, officials and advertisements for its campaign.
4. Appeals to caste, religion and region — canvassing on communal or caste lines, which violates the Model Code of Conduct and divides society.
5. Misinformation — paid news, fake news and misuse of social media to mislead voters.
6. The sheer scale of the exercise — a vast electorate spread over a huge and varied territory, needing lakhs of polling stations, personnel and security arrangements, and special effort to reach remote, hilly and naxal-affected areas.
7. Defects in electoral rolls — bogus, duplicate or missing names.

EVMs with VVPAT, expenditure ceilings and observers, the Model Code of Conduct, NOTA and compulsory affidavits by candidates are steps taken to meet these challenges.

subject: Political Science
context: Answer the following questions in brief (any one):
stem: What efforts are undertaken to bring transparency in political process?
solution:
Several efforts have been made to make the political process open and accountable to the people:

1. Right to Information Act, 2005 — any citizen can obtain information about the working of government offices, which exposes irregularities and checks corruption.
2. Compulsory affidavits by candidates — following Supreme Court directions, every candidate must declare his assets and liabilities, educational qualification and pending criminal cases, and this information is made public so that voters can make an informed choice.
3. Control of election expenditure — the Election Commission fixes a ceiling on the expenditure of a candidate, appoints expenditure observers and requires an account of the expenses; political parties must submit annual audited accounts and reports of contributions received.
4. Model Code of Conduct — binding on parties and candidates from the announcement of the election programme, it prevents misuse of official machinery and appeals on caste or communal lines.
5. Reforms in voting — Electronic Voting Machines with VVPAT slips, photo identity cards and photo electoral rolls prevent bogus voting, and the NOTA option lets a voter reject all candidates.
6. Anti-corruption machinery and laws — the Lokpal and Lokayuktas, the Central Vigilance Commission and anti-defection provisions.
7. Free media, social media and voluntary organisations — they publicise the record of leaders and parties and create public awareness.
